Przysucha Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Przysucha, Poland

Not demolished. Przysucha's Jewish cemetery, first documented in 1723, holds deep significance in Hasidic history: Rabbi Awraham of Przysucha, one of the movement's earliest founders in central Poland, was buried here in 1806, followed in 1813 by tzadik Jakow Icchak, founder of the local Hasidic dynasty, and generations of his family afterward. By 1921, 2,153 Jews made up two-thirds of the town's population, most murdered at Treblinka in 1942. That year, victims of local shootings - including 11 Judenrat members and 19 people killed in the community board's courtyard - were buried here in mass graves, while Germans repurposed tombstones to pave streets and build a gendarmerie station. Poland formally closed the cemetery in 1955, describing it as completely devastated with the last funeral recorded in 1942; the site was later used as a school gymnasium. In the 1980s, Hasidic communities funded two adjoining ohels and a new fence.
